defaults.heading: The answers we'd want ^if it were our account.^

items.body: Your Google, Microsoft, Meta and ChatGPT ad accounts stay in your name, with you as owner. We are granted access, and you can revoke it from your own account settings without losing a day of history. Same for the domain, the phone numbers, and the content.

We ask for read-only access to start, on the ad accounts and analytics. Write access comes only after onboarding, and only for what you have agreed to. We do not need, and do not ask for, access to your CRM billing, payroll, or customer records beyond the lead data you route to us.

The agents are driven through Claude and local harnesses. Your account data is used to do your work — inspect, research, draft — and is not sold, shared with other clients, or used to train a third-party model. Which model runs a given job is an implementation detail; the approval gate does not change with it.

Every consequential change is approved by a named person at GoLumin before it applies. Approvers do not approve their own proposals. The name, the timestamp and the agent's original reasoning stay attached to the change.

Caps are enforced at the apply gate, in code, not by policy. A proposal over the per-change cap is blocked and shown to you as blocked — an approval does not override it. You set the caps during onboarding and can lower them at any time.

Applied changes, rejected proposals and blocked ones all stay on the record, with the evidence that was attached at the time. Clients who want to see the queue get access to their own account's history.

One switch pauses every agent on your account, instantly, without a support ticket. If you leave, the ad accounts are already yours, the content is portable, and the URLs are yours. We do not hold anything hostage as leverage on a renewal.

We keep lead and change records for as long as you are a client and for a reasonable period afterwards so the history stays intact. Ask and we will delete what is ours to delete. See the privacy page for the formal version.

defaults.heading: Privacy
defaults.body:
This page is operated by GoLumin (Martin Business Consultants), a marketing agency that builds and runs Lumin Ads and Lumin CMS. It exists to let you request a free audit.

## What we collect

When you submit the audit form we store the name, email address, business, website, ad spend range and message you enter, together with campaign attribution such as UTM parameters and ad click identifiers, the page you landed on, and the referring site. This lands in our own Lumin lead inbox and is used to reply to you and to measure which campaigns bring demo requests.

## Analytics and advertising tags

The page may load Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics, Google Ads conversion tracking and the Meta pixel. These set cookies and report page views and conversions to those providers under their own privacy policies. You can block them with your browser settings or an ad blocker; the form still works.

## What we do not do

We do not sell your information. We do not add you to an automated email sequence. A person replies.

## Retention and your rights

Demo requests are kept while we work with you or for up to 24 months, whichever is longer. Email [marketing@golumin.io](mailto:marketing@golumin.io) to ask what we hold about you, to correct it, or to have it deleted.

This page is operated by GoLumin (Martin Business Consultants), a marketing agency that builds and runs Lumin Ads and Lumin CMS. It exists to let you request a free audit.

## What we collect

When you submit the audit form we store the name, email address, business, website, ad spend range and message you enter, together with campaign attribution such as UTM parameters and ad click identifiers, the page you landed on, and the referring site. This lands in our own Lumin lead inbox and is used to reply to you and to measure which campaigns bring demo requests.

## Analytics and advertising tags

The page may load Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics, Google Ads conversion tracking and the Meta pixel. These set cookies and report page views and conversions to those providers under their own privacy policies. You can block them with your browser settings or an ad blocker; the form still works.

## What we do not do

We do not sell your information. We do not add you to an automated email sequence. A person replies.

## Retention and your rights

Demo requests are kept while we work with you or for up to 24 months, whichever is longer. Email [marketing@golumin.io](mailto:marketing@golumin.io) to ask what we hold about you, to correct it, or to have it deleted.

entries.title: ChatGPT Ads are one click away in Shopify. Launching them was never the hard part.

frontmatter.lede: OpenAI shipped a free Shopify app that syncs your catalog and builds campaigns from it. It works. But ChatGPT Ads has no dry run, no atomic writes, and no conversions in its performance endpoint, and each of those quietly breaks a habit you brought from Google.
frontmatter.description: OpenAI's free Shopify app puts your catalog into ChatGPT Ads in a few clicks. Three properties of the API decide whether those campaigns actually run. Here they are.
frontmatter.author: GoLumin
frontmatter.og_line: The API said success. The ad never ran.

entries.body_markdown:
On 3 September 2026 OpenAI published its own app to the Shopify App Store. Free, and it does the obvious things well: syncs your catalog into ChatGPT Ads Manager, builds campaigns from it in a few clicks, wires conversion tracking through your Shopify pixels, and keeps reporting inside the Shopify admin. International markets followed on 23 September. The catalog format is the same feed you send to Google Shopping, so there is nothing to rebuild.

If you sell on Shopify in the US, click it. This post is about day four, when the campaign is live and the numbers look wrong, because ChatGPT Ads has three structural properties the Google playbook does not account for. Every one fails quietly.

## 1. “Applied” does not mean “running”

Google Ads gives you `validate_only`: send a change, the API says whether it would be accepted, then you commit. Policy review happens up front.

ChatGPT Ads has no dry run. The ad applies immediately, and policy review lands afterwards, asynchronously.

This is the most expensive failure mode on the platform. Your change succeeded. The API returned success. The dashboard says live. And the ad is not serving, because review rejected it twenty minutes later and nothing told you. The budget sits there looking healthy because nothing is spending it.

*Two lanes, one clock. The left is everything the apply path can tell you; the right is what the ad is actually doing. They agree for about twenty minutes.*

**What Lumin Ads does.** We treat review as a separate axis from status, because it is one: the change applied, the ad just may not be serving. After every apply we poll the verdict with backoff and write it back. A rejection flips the change to `REVIEW_REJECTED` and notifies whoever proposed it, and it is the first thing our agents check on the next run. No point optimising an ad that was never eligible to serve.

We also validate before proposing. ChatGPT publishes an OpenAPI schema, so required fields, enums, limits and reference integrity are checkable before anything is queued. A schema failure here is definitive, so it goes back for revision rather than being sent.

## 2. A failed change can leave you with half a campaign

Google sends one `mutate_operations` call that wholly succeeds or wholly fails. One transaction.

ChatGPT Ads is per-resource REST. A campaign with an ad group and an ad is three separate HTTP calls, and any one can fail. Lose the last and you have a campaign and an ad group that exist, no ad, and a budget attached. Nothing serving, nothing obviously broken, and the error names only the call that failed. Iterate a few times and you accumulate orphaned scaffolding.

*One transaction against three HTTP calls. The failure lands between the calls, which is a place Google's API does not have.*

**What Lumin Ads does.** Every change runs with compensation. If a plan fails partway we archive everything created during that run in reverse order, children before parents, and report exactly what was undone and what was left behind. A rollback that itself fails is reported rather than swallowed, naming the resources still live. You are never told “done” when the truth is “partly”.

It is also why our propose tools bundle: proposing a campaign takes the first ad group and ad with it, so one approval produces something that can serve. Three separate approvals is three chances to strand a half-built structure.

entries.body_markdown:
Shopify and Meta are [partnering to let Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, browse Shopify-powered stores and complete purchases](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/shopify-partners-meta-muse-ai-115807895.html), built on Shop Pay. Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke called it an “easy and delightful way to shop and check out with Muse.” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg put the pitch even shorter: “Shoppers find more. Shops sell more.”

The detail that matters for a store owner is the one Deutsche Bank flagged via the Wall Street Journal: AI platforms keep choosing to work *inside* Shopify’s infrastructure — Shopify Catalog organising the product data, Shop Pay handling payment and delivery, Shopify handling the back-end of the order. The agent is new. What it reads before it buys is everything you already own.

## This is not another ad placement

Our last post was about [ChatGPT Ads arriving one click away in Shopify](/blog/chatgpt-ads-shopify): same feed, new placement, and three API properties that broke the Google playbook. This is the step after that one. There, the AI showed the ad. Here, the AI is the shopper — it browses, compares, and checks out on the customer’s behalf.

Muse launched earlier this month as a personal agent for everyday tasks, on iOS, Android, the web and WhatsApp, with tiers from free to $20 and $100 a month. Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang says the Shopify integration exists to give Muse users “a wide range of stores to find the absolute perfect products.” Translation: when a customer asks Muse to find something, Muse picks from stores it can understand and check out from without friction.

## The merchant landscape just split in two

Amazon [moved to block Muse from buying on its site](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/shopify-partners-meta-muse-ai-115807895.html), warning that an unauthorised agent violates its conditions of use. Shopify did the opposite: a cooperative path, with merchant consent built in through Shop Pay’s existing infrastructure.

That split is the whole story for independent stores. The biggest marketplace opted out. The platform most of you run on opted in, with the checkout your customers already trust. Shopify closed up 7.3% on the news, Meta up 11.4% — the market thinks this lane stays open.

## What Muse reads before it buys

Nobody outside Meta and Shopify has the ranking formula. But the inputs are named in the announcement itself, and every one is something a store can fix this week:

1. **Your catalog.** Deutsche Bank’s read is blunt: what Shopify does well here is organising product data through Shopify Catalog. Titles, descriptions, images, variants, prices, availability — that is what Muse compares when it looks for the “absolute perfect product.” Thin titles and stale availability don’t get clicked less. They get skipped entirely.
2. **Your checkout.** The integration runs on Shop Pay, which holds the customer’s payment and delivery details. If your store checks out cleanly through Shop Pay today, you are already in the lane. If checkout needs a human to coax it — broken shipping rules, mystery fees at the last step, a payment method that fails on mobile — an agent bounces the same way a person does, only faster and without telling you.
3. **Your signal back.** Muse users buy conversationally, which means your reporting has to tie the sale to the session that caused it. Sold outcomes fed back to the ad platforms is already how our clients teach Google and Meta what a customer looks like. Conversational buying makes that feedback loop more important, not less.
4. **Your Meta presence.** Muse lives inside Meta’s apps. Stores Meta already understands — active catalog, honest creative, conversion history — start from a file that exists rather than a cold introduction.

None of this is exotic. It is the unglamorous product-data and checkout work that separates stores that get picked by an agent from stores the agent quietly passes over.

## What Lumin stewards

This is the work we already do for ecommerce clients, pointed at a new buyer who happens to be software:

- **Feed and catalog discipline.** We keep the product data an agent reads accurate and complete — titles that describe the thing, images that show it, prices and availability that match the checkout. The same feed discipline our ChatGPT Ads work depends on.
- **One portfolio, Meta included.** We run Google, Meta, Microsoft and ChatGPT as one governed portfolio, not four logins. Meta is already in the queue we watch every day, so Muse shopping arrives as a new lane on a road we drive, not a new country.
- **Agents that look, humans that sign.** Our agents work the accounts around the clock — cutting waste, pacing budget, flagging stale creative — and every consequential change waits for a named person to approve. Spend caps are enforced in software at the moment of applying, and no approver can override them.
- **Sold, not just spent.** Calls and forms land in your inbox, and marking a lead sold or lost goes back to the platforms as an offline conversion. When Muse starts originating orders, that verdict is what teaches bidding the difference between traffic and customers.

## What we don’t do

We do not have a Shopify app, and the distinction matters — same as with ChatGPT Ads.

Your catalog reaches Muse through Shopify Catalog and Shop Pay. That part is yours and Shopify’s, and it is better than anything we would build to duplicate it. What we steward is everything around it: the data the agent reads, the campaigns that put you in front of the customer before they ask an agent, the conversion signal that teaches the platforms, and the approval gate in front of all of it.

So the honest recommendation is: keep your store on Shopify’s rails, switch on Shop Pay if you haven’t, clean the catalog, then decide separately whether you want someone watching the lane.

## If you want us to look first

We will audit an existing store and ad account before you commit to anything. Read-only access, real findings — catalog gaps, checkout friction, broken conversion tracking, wasted spend — and you keep them whether or not you hire us. If you already sell on Shopify, the first thing we will tell you is what Muse would read about you today.

Most stores are surprised by the answer.

entries.title: What an AI agent actually is, and why marketing without one is a dead end in 2026

frontmatter.lede: Every agency you talk to this year will say the word "agents". Most cannot tell you what one is. Here is the version without the jargon, and the arithmetic behind why it matters.
frontmatter.description: An AI agent is not a chatbot and not automation. The difference in plain English, why it decides whether your marketing gets looked at, and what to demand from an agency.
frontmatter.author: GoLumin
frontmatter.og_line: Automation follows instructions. An agent forms an opinion.

entries.body_markdown:
## Start with a thermostat

Your thermostat holds 68 degrees, and it is very good at this. Somebody leaves a window open in January and it will heat the street until March without ever mentioning it. It is not broken. “Check whether a window is open” was never in the rule.

A person on the night shift walks past the same window and tells you. They are not smarter than the thermostat about temperature. They were looking at something nobody told them to look at.

*The thermostat is not wrong about temperature. It is right, and it will stay right all winter. The difference is the field of view.*

That gap is the whole idea, and it is worth one line:

> **Automation follows instructions. An agent forms an opinion.**

Everything below is that sentence, unpacked.

## Three kinds of software you have already met

You have used all three. Only the names are unfamiliar.

**A tool** does nothing until you pick it up. Your CRM, a spreadsheet, the photo editor nobody on staff knows how to use. Every action is yours. Stop touching it and nothing happens, which is why most software a business buys ends up unused.

**Automation** is a rule you wrote down once. *When a form is submitted, email me. If spend passes $100, pause the campaign.* Fast, reliable, and blind. It does exactly what you specified, forever, including long after the situation changed and the rule became wrong.

**An agent** has a job rather than a rule. You give it a goal, access to look at things, and a schedule. It goes and looks, works out what is wrong, and writes up what it thinks should be done about it.

*The same frame three times. Only the middle row changes, and only the third one comes back with something nobody asked for.*

## What one does on a Tuesday

An agent on a website has one standing job. Say: *find pages that have gone stale, thin or broken*. It runs on a schedule, the way a shift works.

Tuesday morning it reads the site the way a search engine does. It finds a service page untouched in fourteen months, still listing a price you stopped charging in March. It finds a contact form that has been silently failing since a plugin update. It finds that no page answers a question your customers ask constantly.

Then it writes that up: what it found, what it wants to change, the evidence, and what it is worth.

And then it stops. Because the interesting part of an agent is not what it can do. It is what it is not allowed to do.

*Our own console, mid-shift: two agents in flight and the last four runs with what each came back with. The red row failed on an API quota and scheduled its own retry, which is worth showing rather than hiding.*

## The question you should actually be asking

Every owner arrives at the same worry, and it is the right one: *so this thing is making decisions about my money while I sleep?*

The answer depends entirely on the agency. Pin it down before you sign anything.

Ours have read access and no ability to apply anything. They inspect, research, draft and propose. They cannot publish a page, change an ad, or move a dollar. Every consequential change is written up and handed to a named person who signs or rejects it, never their own work, and their name stays on the record next to the change.

Underneath that, spend caps are enforced in code at the moment of applying. A change that would exceed the cap cannot apply **even when a human has already approved it**. The approver cannot override it either. That is the difference between a limit and a promise.

You also get one switch that pauses every agent on your account, instantly.

The useful way to picture an agent is not a robot. It is a new hire in their first month: quick, tireless, reads absolutely everything, and not allowed to sign anything.

*Three changes an agent wrote up, waiting on a person. Nothing here has been applied: a bidding change, fourteen negative keywords and a budget increase, each with the account it belongs to and how long it has waited.*

If an agency cannot tell you clearly what their AI can change without a person, that is not a detail they are glossing over. It is the whole product.

## Why 2026 and not 2015

The argument is not that the software got clever. It is arithmetic.

Marketing used to fit in one head. A twelve-page website. A Google listing. One ad account. A competent person could look at all of it in a week.

Today we run sites with **632 pages**, one for every town and zip code a client delivers to. We migrated a law firm with **324 URLs**. A clinic publishes **75 treatment pages**, each with its own price. On top of that: a business profile wanting posts, photos, hours and answers. Details that must agree across Google, Bing, Apple Maps, Yelp and dozens of directories. Ad accounts on Google, Meta, Microsoft, and now ChatGPT.

The number of things that can quietly be wrong went up a hundredfold. **The number of hours in a retainer did not.**

*One square per page. Left is a brochure site of the kind a small business had a decade ago; right is Inbox Portable Storage's live sitemap today. Not a bar chart, because on a shared axis the left bar is two pixels tall.*

Try this honestly. Take what you pay your agency each month. Divide it by an hourly rate you would consider fair for a competent marketer. That is roughly how many hours your entire marketing gets looked at, by anybody, in a month.

Now ask that many hours to check 632 pages, forty directory listings and four ad platforms. It cannot be done, and it never has been. Not because agencies are lazy. The arithmetic does not work.

So an agency without agents **samples**. It does the handful of things it can reach, and everything else goes unlooked-at until somebody complains.

## You have already lived the consequence

You found it yourself. The contact form broken for six weeks, which you discovered because a customer mentioned they had tried to reach you. The Google listing saying you were closed on Saturdays for most of a year. The ad group that spent $1,400 on a search term that was never going to buy. The page still advertising last spring’s offer.

Not one of those was difficult. Every one is obvious the moment somebody looks. They were not failures of skill or strategy.

**They were failures of attention.** Nobody was looking at that thing on that day.

Attention is what agents supply. Not cleverer than your marketer. Never not looking. Eight of them, one job each, on a standing rota: technical sweep daily, metadata and internal links weekly, content gaps and structured data monthly.

## AI answers punish inconsistency

There is a reason this got urgent this year.

When somebody googled you they got ten links and used their own judgment. If your Yelp hours disagreed with your website, it was untidy and a human worked it out.

When somebody asks ChatGPT for a plumber, a lawyer, a storage unit, they get **one answer** with a couple of businesses named. That answer is assembled from what the internet consistently agrees about you. No second page, and no judgment applied on your behalf.

Disagreement used to be untidy. Now it is a reason to be left out.

Keeping dozens of surfaces in agreement forever, checking for the one directory with your old suite number, is high-volume, low-judgment, never-finished work. Exactly what humans are worst at and most expensive for.

## What agents are bad at

An agent does not know what your business wants this quarter. It does not know you are moving away from the low-margin work, or that the new location matters more than the established one. It has no taste. It cannot tell you which leads were worth having, and **only you know that**. It cannot hold a relationship, negotiate, or decide strategy.

## Start with a thermostat

Your thermostat holds 68 degrees, and it is very good at this. Somebody leaves a window open in January and it will heat the street until March without ever mentioning it. It is not broken. “Check whether a window is open” was never in the rule.

A person on the night shift walks past the same window and tells you. They are not smarter than the thermostat about temperature. They were looking at something nobody told them to look at.

data.caption: The thermostat is not wrong about temperature. It is right, and it will stay right all winter. The difference is the field of view.

data.body:
That gap is the whole idea, and it is worth one line:

> **Automation follows instructions. An agent forms an opinion.**

Everything below is that sentence, unpacked.

## Three kinds of software you have already met

You have used all three. Only the names are unfamiliar.

**A tool** does nothing until you pick it up. Your CRM, a spreadsheet, the photo editor nobody on staff knows how to use. Every action is yours. Stop touching it and nothing happens, which is why most software a business buys ends up unused.

**Automation** is a rule you wrote down once. *When a form is submitted, email me. If spend passes $100, pause the campaign.* Fast, reliable, and blind. It does exactly what you specified, forever, including long after the situation changed and the rule became wrong.

**An agent** has a job rather than a rule. You give it a goal, access to look at things, and a schedule. It goes and looks, works out what is wrong, and writes up what it thinks should be done about it.

data.caption: The same frame three times. Only the middle row changes, and only the third one comes back with something nobody asked for.

data.body:
## What one does on a Tuesday

An agent on a website has one standing job. Say: *find pages that have gone stale, thin or broken*. It runs on a schedule, the way a shift works.

Tuesday morning it reads the site the way a search engine does. It finds a service page untouched in fourteen months, still listing a price you stopped charging in March. Then it writes that up: what it found, what it wants to change, the evidence, and what it is worth.

And then it stops. Because the interesting part of an agent is not what it can do. It is what it is not allowed to do.

data.caption: Our own console, mid-shift: two agents in flight and the last four runs with what each came back with. The red row failed on an API quota and scheduled its own retry, which is worth showing rather than hiding.

## The question you should actually be asking

Every owner arrives at the same worry, and it is the right one: *so this thing is making decisions about my money while I sleep?*

Ours have read access and no ability to apply anything. They inspect, research, draft and propose. They cannot publish a page, change an ad, or move a dollar. data.caption: Three changes an agent wrote up, waiting on a person. Nothing here has been applied: a bidding change, fourteen negative keywords and a budget increase, each with the account it belongs to and how long it has waited.

data.caption: One square per page. Left is a brochure site of the kind a small business had a decade ago; right is Inbox Portable Storage's live sitemap today. Not a bar chart, because on a shared axis the left bar is two pixels tall.

Try this honestly. Take what you pay your agency each month. Divide it by an hourly rate you would consider fair for a competent marketer. That is roughly how many hours your entire marketing gets looked at, by anybody, in a month.
